rules.title: Every goroutine has a way to end
rules.what: A goroutine started in a loop or a handler has a termination path: a propagated context, a bounded worker pool or an errgroup that is waited on.
rules.why: A goroutine with no cancellation keeps its stack, its closures and whatever it blocks on after the work that needed it is gone; a leak that grows with traffic ends as an out-of-memory restart.
rules.how: Pass a context.Context and select on ctx.Done(); use errgroup.WithContext or a fixed-size worker pool; bound the channel that feeds the workers.

patterns.note: Goroutine start; check that it can end. Files that already use context, errgroup, a WaitGroup or a done channel stay silent.

verify.how: A goleak (or runtime.NumGoroutine) check shows the goroutine count back at baseline after the request or test ends.

rules.title: Events, not sleep loops
rules.what: Do not schedule work with time.Sleep in a loop; drive it from a channel, a stoppable ticker, a webhook or a queue.
rules.why: A sleep-and-poll loop spends CPU and network on its own schedule whether or not anything changed, and keeps the machine out of low-power states.
rules.how: Use a channel or a queue; when polling is unavoidable, use time.NewTicker with Stop(), widen the interval and document the stop condition.

patterns.note: time.Sleep; legitimate as retry backoff. Files using a ticker, a select or a timeout context stay silent.

verify.how: The loop is replaced by an event source, or the polling interval and stop condition are documented and justified.

rules.title: Close every response body
rules.what: Close every HTTP response body with defer resp.Body.Close() right after the error check, on every path.
rules.why: An unclosed body keeps its connection out of the pool: the pool opens another one, repeats the TLS handshake, and file descriptors pile up until the process runs out.
rules.how: defer resp.Body.Close() immediately after if err != nil; drain the body (io.Copy(io.Discard, ...)) before closing when the connection must be reused.

patterns.note: HTTP call in a file that never closes a body; files that close one anywhere stay silent, so check each call when there are several.

verify.how: A test with an httptest server shows no growth of open connections across repeated calls.

rules.title: Stream bodies, bound reads
rules.what: Decode from the reader or copy in blocks instead of io.ReadAll on responses, requests and files; bound any read of external input.
rules.why: io.ReadAll allocates memory proportional to the payload; on a large or attacker-controlled body that is a memory spike a stream would have avoided with a fixed buffer.
rules.how: json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&v), io.Copy to the destination, io.LimitReader or http.MaxBytesReader to cap external input.

patterns.note: Whole-payload read; fine for small bounded inputs, candidate for streaming otherwise.

verify.how: A test with a payload larger than the expected maximum shows bounded memory or a clean rejection.

rules.title: One shared HTTP client with timeouts
rules.what: Build one http.Client per service (with Timeout and transport limits) and share it; never build a client per call.
rules.why: A client created per request loses its connection pool: every call redoes DNS and the TLS handshake. A client with no timeout can hold a goroutine and a connection forever.
rules.how: Declare the client at package or service level with Timeout set; use http.NewRequestWithContext with a context.WithTimeout for per-call deadlines.

patterns.note: http.Client built inside a function; a package-level var is the recommendation and is not flagged.
Request without context; files that use NewRequestWithContext, a timeout context or a client Timeout stay silent.

verify.how: The client is created once, has a Timeout, and every request carries a context deadline.

rules.title: Profile before tuning
rules.what: Validate CPU, heap and blocking changes with pprof and benchmarks; do not raise GOMAXPROCS, parallelism or add sync.Pool without workload evidence.
rules.why: Allocation and concurrency tweaks made without a profile often add complexity for no measurable gain, and can worsen contention or memory.
rules.how: go test -bench with -benchmem, pprof CPU/heap/block profiles before and after; check escape analysis (-gcflags=-m) before changing allocations.

verify.how: Before/after benchmark or profile attached to the change, on a representative workload.
